## What is the lead paint indicator?

The "lead paint indicator" is based on the percentage of housing units
built before 1960, a proxy for how much lead-based paint people might be
exposed to. EJScreen presents this potential exposure to lead-based
paint using percentile rank, ranging from 0 (lowest) to 100 (highest)
with higher scores representing higher potential for exposure.

## Why is lead paint important?

- Lead-based paint, often present in older homes built before 1978, is
  one of the most common ways in which people can be exposed to lead.
- Lead-based paint becomes a hazard when people have direct contact with
  peeling painted surfaces or released lead particles, since lead may
  then adhere to their hands and other parts of their bodies, and some
  portion of the lead may be ingested. If the painted surfaces are
  disturbed through home renovation, repair, or painting activities,
  some lead-based paint particles may become temporarily suspended in
  the air as lead dust, then may be inhaled or ingested after falling on
  food. Children may be exposed to lead dust when they put their hands
  or objects into their mouths as part of their normal hand-to-mouth
  behavior.
- Lead is especially dangerous to children under the age of six because
  their growing bodies absorb more lead than adults. Even low levels of
  lead exposure to children can result in damage to the brain and
  nervous system; delayed growth and development; behavior and learning
  problems; lower IQ; speech and hearing problems; and hyperactivity.

## How does EJScreen create the lead paint indicator?

- The percentage of older housing units is used as a proxy for potential
  exposure to lead-based paint and lead-containing dust that accumulates
  indoors, in homes, or in other buildings where lead-based paint was
  used. EJScreen uses the percentage of housing stock built before 1960
  because regulations banning lead-based residential paint in 1978 led
  to the reduction and finally an end to the use of such paint in
  housing. The decision for EJScreen to use housing units built before
  1960 is based on Jacobs et al., 2002.
- The housing stock data are derived from the [American Community Survey
  (ACS) 5-year
  Summary](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/acs-5year.html)
  block group-level estimates.

## Moving Forward – What You Can Do

- Protect yourself and your family from exposure to lead:
  - The EPA [Actions to Reduce Potential Lead
    Exposure](/lead/actions-reduce-potential-lead-exposure) webpage
    (also [available in
    Spanish](https://espanol.epa.gov/plomo/acciones-para-reducir-la-exposicion-al-plomo))
    provides helpful information on preventing lead exposure and lead
    poisoning, especially in young children.
  - The EPA's [Protect Your Family from Lead in Your
    Home](/lead/protect-your-family-lead-your-home-real-estate-disclosure#12)
    pamphlet, which explains the dangers of lead in your home and how to
    protect your family from lead-based paint hazards. This pamphlet is
    required to be provided to prospective buyers and renters of
    pre-1978 homes and is available in multiple languages.
  - [Lead-based inspections and lead risk
    assessments](/lead/lead-abatement-inspection-and-risk-assessment)
    are useful first steps to determine whether lead-based paint is
    present in a home and to address lead-based paint hazards. These can
    lead to thoughtful decisions on managing lead-based paint and lead
    hazards in homes.
  - Know your rights before you buy or lease housing and your
    responsibilities before you sell or lease housing by reviewing
    information on the EPA's [Real Estate Disclosures about Potential
    Lead
    Hazard](/lead/real-estate-disclosures-about-potential-lead-hazards)s.
  - [Learn about Lead Laws and
    Regulations](/lead/lead-laws-and-regulations).
  - Work with your local leaders to identify lead issues and develop an
    action plan using the [Local Lead Action Plan
    Guide](/lead/llap-guide).
- Learn more about how the EPA and others continue to reduce lead-based
  paint exposure in communities:
  - The EPA's [Strategy to Reduce Lead Exposures and Disparities in U.S.
    Communities](/lead/final-strategy-reduce-lead-exposures-and-disparities-us-communities)
    advances the Agency's work to protect the public from lead with an
    emphasis on high-risk communities.
  - The EPA [Lead Exposures Page](/lead) provides an extensive
    assortment of resources, educational documents, and outreach
    materials for protecting the public from harmful lead exposures,
    including exposure from lead in homes, water, air, soil, and
    consumer products.
  - The EPA's publications on [Data Mapping to Identify High Lead
    Exposure Risk Locations](/lead/mapping) are available for local,
    state, and federal government officials to identify high lead
    exposure risk locations and communities.
  - Learn about the EPA's [Lead Renovation, Repair and Painting (RRP)
    Program](/lead/lead-renovation-repair-and-painting-program) which
    requires that RRP projects that disturb lead-based paint in homes,
    childcare facilities, and preschools built before 1978 be performed
    by lead-safe certified contractors.
  - The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's [Childhood Lead
    Poisoning Prevention
    Program](https://www.cdc.gov/lead-prevention/php/about-clppp/index.html)
    is dedicated to eliminating childhood lead poisoning as a public
    health problem and supports [state and local health
    departments](https://www.cdc.gov/lead-prevention/success-stories-by-state/index.html).
  - The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's (HUD) [Office
    of Lead Hazard Control and Healthy
    Homes](https://www.hud.gov/program_offices/healthy_homes) provides
    funds to state and local governments to reduce lead-based paint
    hazards, enforces lead-based paint regulations, provides public
    outreach and technical assistance, and conducts studies to protect
    children and their families. HUD's [About Lead-based Paint
    Page](https://www.hud.gov/program_offices/healthy_homes/healthyhomes/lead)
    provides tips and resources.
- Attend a [Community Lead Awareness
  Session](/lead/community-lead-awareness-sessions) in
  [English](/lead/community-lead-awareness-sessions) or
  [Spanish](https://espanol.epa.gov/plomo/conciencia-comunitaria-sobre-el-plomo).
  The EPA is partnering with communities across the country to host a
  series of free educational sessions on the dangers of lead and how to
  reduce and prevent lead exposure.

## References

Jacobs, D. E., *et al*., 2002. *The Prevalence of Lead-Based Paint
Hazards in U.S. Housing*. Environ Health Prospect, 110(10), a599-a606.
